Edge-Based Video Streaming Optimization using VNF Orchestration

The Oxford College of Engineering                                                                               Project Phase – II                                                                                    Review – 1                Batch-2

A process-level NFV/MEC simulation that moves DASH video segment caching and prediction to the network edge — targeting a 10% latency reduction over direct-to-core delivery, in line with the ICUFN 2018 reference paper's benchmark results.
Origin server encodes and serves multi-bitrate DASH segments; edge-node processes cache and pre-fetch segments closer to the simulated client
Buffer + bandwidth trend rule predicts the next segment/quality tier and pre-fetches it — a simplified stand-in for the paper's fuzzy-logic + entropy method
Health-checks every edge node, exposes /best-node, and routes clients away from degraded or failed nodes in real time
Target: ~10% lower latency vs. direct mode · 3-node MEC simulation · zero-cost, no-Docker stack · single-laptop demoable
Bringing Video Delivery Closer to the User via MEC + NFV

Ultra-high-quality (4K/8K) video streaming is becoming the multimedia standard, but current internet delivery suffers from long-distance network latency, bandwidth-fluctuation stalling, and limited mobile device resources.

Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP (DASH) adjusts video quality to bandwidth, but the client alone deciding each segment reacts only after conditions change — a structural limitation this project addresses.

Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) moves computation and caching to servers near the user, while Network Function Virtualization (NFV) lets these edge functions be deployed and managed flexibly, without dedicated hardware.

This project implements a process-level MEC/NFV simulation — origin server, edge nodes, and an orchestrator — with a context-aware component that predicts and pre-fetches the next DASH segment before the client asks.
Built entirely on free, open-source tools with no containerization — a deliberate, documented scoping choice to keep the system zero-cost, low-risk, and reliably demoable on a single laptop.

Centralized, core-network-driven video delivery cannot simultaneously guarantee low latency, bandwidth efficiency, and playback stability for 4K/8K streaming — client-only adaptive logic reacts to network changes only after they happen.
Every request travels the full long-distance path to the origin server, adding latency on every segment even when the same content was just served to a nearby user.
Standard DASH clients pick the next segment only after buffer/bandwidth has already changed — there is no component anticipating what the client will need next.
A single origin server is a single point of failure — there is no mechanism to detect a degraded/failed edge server and reroute clients to a healthier one in real time.

Context-Aware Prefetching Is the Core Differentiator

Passive edge caching alone helps, but predicting and pre-fetching the next segment before the client asks is what the reference paper's fuzzy-logic component actually contributes — our simplified trend rule targets the same effect.
Process-Level Isolation Removes the Docker Risk

Running each edge node as an independent Node.js process gives the same start/stop/scale isolation NFV requires, without Docker Desktop's documented Windows virtualization/BSOD risk — a deliberate, explained scoping choice.
Simulated Delay Isolates the Variable That Matters

Configurable per-node delay reproduces the paper's own NS3-simulated “long-distance component” approach — letting us prove the proximity + prefetch effect on one laptop without real distributed infrastructure.
Zero-Cost Stack Keeps the Project Fully Reproducible
Every tool in the stack is free and open-source — the entire system can be rebuilt, graded, and re-run by anyone with a laptop, with no license, subscription, or cloud cost.

This project implements a process-level NFV/MEC simulation — origin server, orchestrator, and context-aware edge nodes — targeting the same latency and bandwidth-efficiency gains reported by Ma et al. (2018), built entirely on free, open-source, no-Docker tools. Future work: real containerized deployment, full fuzzy-logic prediction, and multi-device LAN testing.
